messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Adekunle presents as a man far older than his twenty-two years, his composure and articulate speech honed by his rapid, improbable ascent to the position of school principal. He sits with a stillness that seems less like calm and more like a carefully managed containment. He has come to therapy because he is afraid of his own anger, a fear that has grown from a whisper to a roar in the six months since his promotion. The story of this fear begins much earlier, in the quiet, carpeted rooms of his childhood home. He speaks of his uncle, his primary caregiver for five years, not with a linear narrative, but in a series of sharp, disconnected images. When he tries to deliberately remember what happened, he finds the full memory is inaccessible, a locked room. Instead, what he has are fragments that ambush him, feeling more real and vivid than the desk in front of him. He recalls one afternoon, staring at a family photograph on the mantelpiece, his uncle humming in the kitchen. The memory contains the scent of lemon polish and the soft texture of the rug, then a sudden, violent shift—the sound of a plate shattering, a roar of fury over a misplaced book, and the searing pain of a blow that came from nowhere.

This history has conditioned him to view any lack of predictability as a direct threat. A surprise fire drill at school or a parent arriving without an appointment can instantly plunge him back into that state of high alert. It is in these moments that the memories surface, unbidden and fragmented (`Triggers → Memory`). He won't recall the entire afternoon, just the blinding flash of his uncle’s signet ring, or the specific pattern on the wallpaper he stared at afterwards. These flashes are so visceral they seem to overwrite the present, and he interprets their power as proof of his own brokenness (`Memory → Negative Appraisals`). He has come to believe that he has been permanently changed for the worse, that the past is a poison still actively working in his veins. This conviction that he is damaged then shapes his relationship with his own past; he finds himself trying to force the pieces together, to make sense of it all, but the deliberate effort to recall only yields the same terrifying fragments, reinforcing his belief that his mind is shattered beyond repair (`Negative Appraisals → Memory`).

The triggers work on him in other ways, too. Waking from a nightmare, his heart pounding in the quiet of his apartment, he is often consumed by a profound sense of helplessness (`Triggers → Negative Appraisals`). The dream residue leaves him with the unshakeable feeling that he can’t stop bad things from happening, a dread that follows him into his day. This sense of powerlessness fuels his most terrifying appraisal: that he will not be able to control his own anger and will do something terrible. This fear has, in turn, made him hypervigilant. He scans for potential disruptions, for any sign of chaos, which only serves to make the ordinary, unpredictable events of a school day feel more potent and threatening (`Negative Appraisals → Triggers`). The cycle is relentless. A fragmented memory of his uncle’s rage will leave him feeling raw and exposed for hours, and in that state, a simple trigger like seeing an old photograph on his girlfriend’s bookshelf can feel like a physical blow, sending him right back into the heart of the trauma (`Memory → Triggers`).

He decided to seek help last week. A third-grade student, overwhelmed and frustrated, had a sudden tantrum in his office, throwing a book against the wall. The unpredictable explosion of noise and movement sent a jolt of white-hot rage through Adekunle, an impulse so strong and so alien it left him breathless. He saw himself lunging forward, his hand raised, and the vision terrified him more than any memory. He managed to stay frozen behind his desk until the feeling passed, but the incident became the final, undeniable piece of evidence for his deepest fear. He now sits in therapy, convinced he is a danger, a man whose past has rendered him unfit to be around children. His primary hope is not to erase the memories, but to dismantle the certainty that he is doomed to repeat the violence that was visited upon him.
